headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 1.22 (95% CI: 0.53–2.8), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin A and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 92.67%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

sample_size.excerpt: We examined dietary and other risk factors for renal adenocarcinoma in a case-control study of 203 incident and 207 prevalent cases and 605 neighborhood controls. Using unconditional logistic regression to control selection biases identified in an adjunct study, we found exposure odds ratios (OR) similar to those from other studies: 1.9 (with a 95% confidence interval (Cl) from 0.8 to 4.4) for smoking 2 packs of cigarettes per day; 3.8 (95% Cl: 0.78-18) for 3 or more packs per day; 1.7 (95% Cl: 0.9-3.2) for women and 1.7 (95% Cl: 1.1-2.8) for men in the highest quintile of relative weight (kg/m2); 2.0 (95% Cl: 1.3-3.1) for northeastern European ancestry; and 2.3 (95% Cl: 1.3-4.1) for history of kidney stones.

cases.excerpt: Sociodemographic and baseline health characteristics and nutrient intake levels of 1142 cases and 1154 controls in the eligible study population are presented by race in Table 1 .
